analytic.title: Independent WCRT analysis for the Best-Effort class BE in Ethernet AVB

div.p: Existing papers on worst-case response time analysis for individual classes in Ethernet AVB typically focus on classes under credit-based shaping (CBS). There also exist industrial applications that use the Best-Effort class BE for non-hard realtime traffic with a minimum quality-of-service (QoS) requirement, however. In this paper, we therefore present a conjecture for worst-case response time analysis for that class BE, stating that the existing analysis based on eligible intervals can be equally well applied to a single (highest-priority) stream without CBS, by simply assuming the remaining bandwidth to be available to that stream. The conjecture is illustrated using a figure.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the high-tech and automotive industry, there is a need for high bandwidth communication combined with the possibility to give real-time guarantees through a widely accepted standard. Since the development of the Ethernet AVB standard by the Audio/Video Bridging Task Group 1 , Ethernet became a viable solution to this problem. To be able to guarantee required latencies and throughput, this standard introduced credit-based shaping (CBS) [1] for two traffic classes, i.e. the Stream Reservation (SR) classes A and B. This key flow control approach shapes the outgoing traffic of a switch based on priority scheduling and credit levels.

Most existing worst-case response time analysis of individual messages under CBS [2]- [7] only provide results for the traffic classes A and B, i.e. do not address the (lowest priority) Best-Effort (BE) class. Although BE traffic may not have strict timing requirements, it is typically expected (c.q. required) that it achieves acceptable levels of Quality of Service (QoS) [8], e.g. when the BE class is used to support legacy traffic. Worstcase response time analysis for messages of the BE class has therefore also been addressed in [9], as an extension of [7].

As illustrated in [10], which presents an efficient analysis of bandwidth reservation for CBS, analysis based on so-called eligible intervals [4] typically outperforms the analysis based on busy periods, such as [5], for classes A and B. Moreover, the analysis presented in [4] does not rely on any assumptions This work has been performed in the context of the PENTA Call 3 project 17006 HiPer (High Performance Vehicle Computer and Communication System for Autonomous Driving). 1 The AVB Task Group was renamed to Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) Task Group in November 2012. on interfering priority classes other than those enforced by the Ethernet AVB standard, i.e. it is independent of arrival patterns of interfering classes. Finally, that analysis is considerably simpler and has a linear (instead of a pseudo-polynomial) complexity. Given its merits, we therefore aim at extending the work in [4] (and its generalization to more than three streams in [6]) with analysis for class BE in this paper. To that end, we present a conjecture stating that the worst-case response time analysis for individual messages of class BE can simply be determined using the existing analysis by assuming that the BE class receives the remaining bandwidth under CBS. The conjecture is illustrated using a figure.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we present a basic system model for Ethernet AVB. A recap of worst-case response time analysis based on eligible intervals is presented in Section III. We present and illustrate our conjecture in Section IV. In Section V, the paper is concluded.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In this section, we model the behavior at the output port of a single switch that is part of an Ethernet AVB network, with a focus on CBS [11] and using the notation of [6].

As a basis, Ethernet AVB adopts non-preemptive strict priority scheduling, where frames of the same priority class are treated in a FIFO manner. On top of this, Ethernet AVB adds a CBS mechanism for the (highest) priority classes to limit traffic bursts. Credit for a priority class X under CBS starts at 0 (zero). A frame of X can only start its transmission if X has non-negative credit. While a frame is transmitted, the credit drops at a rate of α - X . If credit is negative, no further frames can be transmitted and credit rises with a rate of α + X . Credit also rises at a rate of α + X if X has pending frames but cannot transmit. Positive credit is reset to 0 if is X has no pending frames.

We assume a totally ordered set P of (at least) three priority classes, e.g. A, B, and BE of AVB; see also the left panel of Figure 1, where A, B, and BE are denoted by H, M , and L, respectively. A generalization to more than three classes is illustrated in the right panel of Figure 1. For X, Y ∈ P, we write X < Y to indicate that X has a lower priority than Y . The set P can be partitioned in two subsets, P CBS and P SP , where SP in P SP denotes strict priority transmission selection [11]. Only traffic classes in P CBS are subject to bandwidth reservation. Both P CBS and P SP contain at least one class 2 , and all classes in P CBS have a higher priority than the classes in P SP . We make the following assumptions for a traffic class X ∈ P CBS , where BW represents the total bandwidth
div.formula: ∀ X∈P CBS 0 < α + X ≤ BW ∧ α - X = BW -α + X and X∈P CBS α + X ≤ BW.
div.p: Moreover, for a subset of traffic classes X ⊆ P CBS , we introduce the following notation

div.p: We write x ∈ X to indicate that a frame x is of a priority class X. When discussing the behavior of CBS, we also speak of a stream X when considering the flow of frames from input to transmission. In [6], an axiomatic approach to formally model the dynamics of CBS is followed, in which executions u are considered, and properties are given under which u is a valid execution of a system. We use the same notation here, and write for example CR u X (t) to denote the credit of priority class X at time t ∈ R + during an execution u. We use s u (x) and C u (x) to denote the start time and the transmission time of frame x in execution u, respectively. Finally, the maximum frame size of a stream X is denoted by C max X . The maximum frame size C max X of a set of streams X is therefore given by
div.formula: C max X = max X∈X C max X .

div.head: III. A RECAP OF WORST-CASE RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS
div.p: In this section, the independent worst-case response time analysis for Ethernet AVB as presented in [6] is recapitulated. Next to intra-class interference due to FIFO scheduling of frames of a traffic class, frames of streams that are subject to bandwidth reservation experience two types of delay:
1) intra-class delay induced by CBS of the class itself;

2) inter-class interference, albeit bounded by CBS of higher priority streams. These two types are addressed in the following two subsections. For the intra-class interference due to FIFO scheduling, we refer to, for example, Lemma 1 of [4].

div.head: IV. WCRT ANALYSIS FOR THE HIGHEST-PRIORITY NON-SHAPED CLASS L
div.p: In this section, we present a conjecture claiming that for the highest-priority (non-shaped) class L ∈ P SP the existing analysis based on eligible intervals can be simply be applied, by assuming a bandwidth reservation α + L for L equal to the remaining bandwidth, i.e. with α + L = α - P CBS . We illustrate the conjecture using a figure. The section is concluded with remarks.

div.head: A. A conjecture
div.p: Conjecture 1. Given the highest priority stream L ∈ P SP , we can apply the existing worst-case response time analysis based on eligible intervals also to L, i.e. Corollary 1 and Theorem 3, by simply treating L as a credit-based shaped class with a bandwidth reservation α + L = α - P CBS , where H(L) = P CBS . Given this conjecture, the remaining bandwidth α - P CBS = BW-α + P CBS of P CBS can therefore be viewed as the bandwidth reservation for the best-effort class L to determine the worstcase response times of frames of L.

div.head: C. Concluding remarks
div.p: Note that the amount of data transmitted by L in the interval

div.p: . This is a worst-case (i.e. minimal) amount of data, because we assumed that streams of the classes H(L) were sending data whenever possible and as much as possible. Stream L can therefore effectively sent at least a fraction

BW of the bandwidth. Additional bandwidth comes available to L based on spare bandwidth, i.e. a combination of slack 4 and gain bandwidth 5 . Finally, we observe that L(L) need not be empty. In case L(L) is non-empty, we can simply apply Theorem 3 for the worst-case relative delay by making the same assumption α + L = α - H(L) . Independent worst-case response-time analysis for X ∈ L(L) based on eligible intervals is not possible, however, simply because L may consume all bandwidth left by H(L).

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we presented a conjecture for independent worst-case response time analysis of individual messages of the Best-Effort class BE in Ethernet AVB. The conjecture essentially states that the existing analysis based on eligible intervals [6] can equally well be applied to the class BE by simply assuming that the remaining bandwidth is made available to it under CBS. In case of multiple non-shaped priority classes [11], the conjecture applies to the highest priority nonshaped class. We merely illustrated the conjecture using a figure. We leave a proof of the conjecture and considerations concerning the tightness of the analysis as future work. 4 Slack bandwidth is the amount of bandwidth that has not been allocated to streams, i.e. BW -α + P CBS . 5 Gain bandwidth is bandwidth that has been allocated to streams, but is not used.

Analysis based on eligible intervals has not yet reached the same level of maturity as analysis based on busy periods [7]. Although the combination of CBS and Time-Aware Shapers (TAS) [12] of TSN has been addressed in [13], an extension with preemption support [14] is still uncharted territory. Further extensions of worst-case response time analysis for class BE based on eligible intervals in a context with TAS and preemption support is also future work.
